claims.claim_text: Can't Stop analysis shows four-dice odds flatten the distribution, middle columns dominate, probabilistic stopping wins, and forced moves balance design
claims.evidence_quote: Four-dice probabilities flatten the distribution... Column combinations matter more... Probabilistic strategies dominate... The forced-move rule is brilliant
claims.reasoning: Summary compresses four conclusion-section findings with identical meaning.

claims.claim_text: Push-your-luck rules: roll four dice, pair freely, bust loses turn progress
claims.evidence_quote: roll four dice, pair them up however you want... if you can't move any of your three active markers, you lose everything you've gained that turn
claims.reasoning: All three rule elements stated identically.

claims.claim_text: Board columns 2 to 12 vary 3 to 13 steps; complete three to win
claims.evidence_quote: columns numbered 2 through 12, with different lengths... Columns 2 and 12: 3 steps... Column 7: 13 steps... You need to complete three columns to win
claims.reasoning: Range, extremes, and win condition all exact.

claims.claim_text: Forced-move rule requires taking every legal move from the chosen pairing
claims.evidence_quote: you must take all available moves... you must make ALL legal moves from that pairing, even if you don't want them
claims.reasoning: Near-verbatim restatement of the critical rule.

claims.claim_text: Chasing 7 on {6,7,8} can force an unwanted 2 onto the board
claims.evidence_quote: if you're working on columns {6, 7, 8} and you roll (1,1,3,4)... you're forced to take BOTH the 2 and the 7, even though column 2 isn't in your plan
claims.reasoning: Source example restated with identical columns, roll, and forced outcome.

claims.claim_text: Four-dice pairing flattens the probability distribution versus two dice
claims.evidence_quote: Did the distribution get flatter?... Four-dice probabilities flatten the distribution - P(7) = 64.4% vs P(2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88x difference compared to 6x with two dice
claims.reasoning: Flattening thesis stated in both the analysis question and the conclusion.

claims.claim_text: Two-dice baseline: 7 hits 16.67%, six times more likely than 2
claims.evidence_quote: Sum 7 is the most likely at 16.67%, and it's exactly 6x more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%
claims.reasoning: Percentage and ratio both exact.

claims.claim_text: Four dice yield exactly three possible pairings per roll
claims.evidence_quote: That's it, just three possible pairings
claims.reasoning: Count exact.

claims.claim_text: Making a 2 needs two 1s: 171/1296, about 13.2%
claims.reasoning: Condition, fraction, and percentage all exact.

claims.claim_text: Making a 7 via inclusion-exclusion: 834/1296, about 64.4%
claims.reasoning: Method, fraction, and percentage all exact.

claims.claim_text: Probability ratio 4.88 nearly matches length ratio 4.33; designers thought carefully
claims.evidence_quote: The probability ratio from 2 to 7 is 4.88. The length ratio is 4.33. Pretty close! The game designers were definitely thinking about this
claims.reasoning: Both ratios exact and the designers-thinking inference matches source tone.

claims.claim_text: Column combinations matter more than individual column odds
claims.evidence_quote: Column combinations matter more than individual columns... Column 7 in {6,7,8}: expected completion in ~2 turns
claims.reasoning: Section thesis restated identically.

claims.claim_text: Expected rolls cluster near 20; long column 7 completes slightly faster than 2
claims.evidence_quote: For column 2: 3/0.132 = 22.73 rolls. For column 7: 13/0.644 = 20.18 rolls. Column 7 is slightly faster
claims.reasoning: Clustering near 20 and the 7-faster-than-2 comparison both exact.

claims.claim_text: {6,7,8} succeeds 92% per roll; {2,3,12} only 43.8%
claims.evidence_quote: Result: 1193/1296 = 92.0% success rate... Result: 568/1296 = 43.8% success rate
claims.reasoning: Both success rates exact.

claims.claim_text: 37 combos rate excellent; median succeeds 79.6%, worst collapse to 43.8%
claims.evidence_quote: 37 combinations are excellent (>=85% success rate)... The median combination still succeeds 79.6% of the time, but the worst combinations drop dramatically to just 43.8%
claims.reasoning: All three distribution figures exact.

claims.claim_text: Stopping rule weighs expected gain against bust-weighted unsaved progress
claims.evidence_quote: Keep rolling if: (P_success x Q) > (P_bust x U)
claims.reasoning: Heuristic formula restated with identical variables and meaning.

claims.claim_text: Roll on {6,7,8} with five steps banked; stop on {2,3,12} with two
claims.evidence_quote: Let's test this on {6,7,8} with 5 unsaved steps... Since 1.32 > 0.4, you should keep rolling... on {2,3,12} with 2 unsaved steps... you should STOP
claims.reasoning: Both worked examples with matching columns, stakes, and decisions.

claims.claim_text: Only 39.8% of {6,7,8} rolls are clean; {2,3,12} just 2.3%
claims.evidence_quote: Only 39.8% of rolls give you a clean move on {6,7,8}!... For {2,3,12}: Only 2.3% of rolls are clean!
claims.reasoning: Both clean-move percentages exact.

claims.claim_text: Continuing current columns usually beats switching, but switching unanalyzed quantitatively
claims.evidence_quote: The mathematics favor continuation in most cases... Note: I haven't fully analyzed this aspect quantitatively
claims.reasoning: Continuation leaning plus the explicit quantitative hedge both stated; hedge preserved, not absolutized.

claims.claim_text: 3.6M-game simulations crown probabilistic, consistent strategies over fast ones
claims.evidence_quote: 38 strategies, each playing 2,500 games against every other strategy (3.6 million total games)... Probabilistic strategies dominate
claims.reasoning: Game count exact and the probabilistic-plus-consistency verdict matches the findings sections.

claims.claim_text: 38 strategy families tested across single-player and head-to-head simulations
claims.evidence_quote: I implemented 38 different strategies and ran them against each other... I tested 38 strategies across 14 different strategic families
claims.reasoning: Source counts 38 strategies in 14 families; claim says 38 families. Wrong family count, though the 38 figure itself is real. Conclusions unaffected, so Minor.

claims.claim_text: GreedyUntil1Col fastest at 10.5 turns but busts 7.5 times per game
claims.evidence_quote: GreedyUntil1Col is fastest (10.5 turns) but has high variance... and bust rate (7.5 per game)
claims.reasoning: Speed and bust figures both exact.

claims.claim_text: FiftyPercentSurvival wins 69.84% by stopping below 50% cumulative survival
claims.evidence_quote: FiftyPercentSurvival dominates with 69.84% overall win rate... Roll until cumulative survival probability drops below 50%
claims.reasoning: Win rate and stopping rule both exact.

claims.claim_text: Consistency beats raw speed; pure greedy loses nearly everything
claims.evidence_quote: consistency beats raw speed... The pure Greedy strategy (never stop voluntarily) lost essentially every game
claims.reasoning: Lesson headline and pure-greedy result both stated.

claims.claim_text: First player wins 55.59%, an 11.18% edge exceeding chess and Go
claims.evidence_quote: Player 1 win rate: 55.59%... First-player advantage: +11.18%... larger than chess (~5%) or Go (~7%)
claims.reasoning: All three figures exact.

claims.claim_text: Board is nearly balanced singly; forced moves compensate combination imbalance
claims.evidence_quote: The deviations are +-13.6% at most... rules and mechanics compensate for inevitable imbalances... that compensating rule is the forced-move rule
claims.reasoning: Single-column balance plus forced-move compensation both stated.

claims.claim_text: Single-column completion deviates at most 13.6% from 20 rolls
claims.evidence_quote: The deviations are +-13.6% at most
claims.reasoning: Deviation bound exact.

claims.claim_text: Adding one step per middle column would quadruple balance precision
claims.evidence_quote: 4x more balanced with just +1 step!
claims.reasoning: Fourfold improvement with one added step matches.

claims.claim_text: Forced moves contaminate strong combos, keeping strategy choices interesting
claims.evidence_quote: Forces players into sub-optimal column combinations... Adds tactical complexity... Compensates for the mathematical imbalance
claims.reasoning: Contamination mechanism and interesting-choice consequence both stated.

claims.claim_text: Play middle columns consistently; designers should favor playability over perfection
claims.evidence_quote: Aim for columns 5-9... prioritize consistency over aggressive play... Prioritize playability over mathematical perfection
claims.reasoning: Player and designer takeaways restated identically.

claims.claim_text: Aim for columns 5-9, avoid edge columns, prioritize consistency over aggression
claims.evidence_quote: Aim for columns 5-9, avoid forcing activation of columns 2-3 and 11-12, and prioritize consistency over aggressive play
claims.reasoning: Player advice restated identically.

claims.claim_text: All code, simulations, and datasets are published for reuse
claims.evidence_quote: All analysis code and simulation results are available
claims.reasoning: Code-and-data availability stated with matching artifact list in source.
